claim: There has been a rapid increase in prevalence of myopia, of all magnitudes, in the period between 1971–1972 and 1999–2004.
source: There has been a rapid increase in prevalence of myopia, of all magnitudes, in the period between 1971–1972 and 1999–2004 (Vitale, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vitale, 2009

claim: Axial length of the eye is the primary variable related to myopia across sub-populations grouped by race, ethnicity and gender.
source: Across sub-populations grouped by race, ethnicity and gender, several studies report axial length of the eye to be the primary variable related to myopia (González Blanco et al., 2008; He et al., 2015; Iyamu et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to González Blanco et al., 2008; He et al., 2015; Iyamu et al., 2011

claim: Increased axial length is associated with retinal stretching and thinning of posterior segment layers and the choroid.
source: Increased axial length is associated with retinal stretching and thinning of posterior segment layers and the choroid (Fujiwara et al., 2009; Harb et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to Fujiwara et al., 2009; Harb et al., 2015

claim: Increased axial length is associated with sight-threatening, often irreversible pathologies of the retina.
source: Increased axial length is associated with retinal stretching and thinning of posterior segment layers and the choroid (Fujiwara et al., 2009; Harb et al., 2015) and is associated with sight-threatening, often irreversible pathologies of the retina (Morgan et al., 2012; Verkicharla et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Morgan et al., 2012; Verkicharla et al., 2015

claim: The axial elongation associated with eye growth is accompanied by magnification of the retinal image.
source: However the situation is not that simple; the axial elongation associated with eye growth is accompanied by magnification of the retinal image (Strang et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Strang et al., 1998

claim: In large scale studies, myopes generally attain reasonably good visual acuity with optical correction.
source: In fact, in large scale studies, myopes generally attain reasonably good visual acuity with optical correction (He et al., 2004; Jong et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to He et al., 2004; Jong et al., 2018

claim: Myopes generally (6 out of 9 studies) have poorer angular resolution.
source: However, more careful inspection reveals that myopes generally (6 out of 9 studies) have poorer angular resolution and have uniformly (3 out of 3 studies) poorer retinal resolution.
evidence: Supported by summary of published studies in Table 1

claim: Myopes have uniformly (3 out of 3 studies) poorer retinal resolution.
source: However, more careful inspection reveals that myopes generally (6 out of 9 studies) have poorer angular resolution and have uniformly (3 out of 3 studies) poorer retinal resolution.
evidence: Supported by summary of published studies in Table 1

claim: Atchison et al. (2006) and Coletta and Watson (2006) show clear deficits in retinal resolution (cyc/mm) with increasing myopia using interferometric methods.
source: Most notably, Atchison et al. (2006) and Coletta and Watson (2006) show clear deficits in retinal resolution (cyc/mm) with increasing myopia using interferometric methods which bypass the optics of the eye
evidence: Supported by citations to Atchison et al. (2006) and Coletta and Watson (2006)

claim: Rossi et al. (2007) show significant deficits in angular resolution (cyc/deg) in low myopes, even after using adaptive optics to correct for optical blur.
source: Rossi et al. (2007) show significant deficits in angular resolution (cyc/deg) in low myopes, even after using adaptive optics to correct for optical blur.
evidence: Supported by citation to Rossi et al. (2007)

claim: All studies that find myopic visual deficits implicate retinal stretching as a possible cause.
source: All studies that find myopic visual deficits implicate retinal stretching as a possible cause, but what is actually happening structurally at the foveal center during myopic progression is not known.
evidence: Inferred from review of studies in Table 1

claim: In the global expansion model, linear density decreases with eye length.
source: In the first model, called the global expansion model, the retina is proportionally stretched with increasing axial length - cones are more spaced out in longer eyes - and linear density decreases with eye length.
evidence: Theoretical model illustrated in Figure 1A

claim: In the global expansion model, angular cone density will be constant with eye length.
source: Assuming that the secondary nodal point remains at a fixed position relative to the anterior segment, the number of cones within a fixed angular area will remain constant. Therefore, angular cone density will be constant with eye length.
evidence: Theoretical model illustrated in Figure 1A

claim: In the equatorial stretching model, linear density does not change with eye length.
source: In the second model, called the equatorial stretching model, the posterior retina simply moves axially further from the anterior segment of the eye so that the linear density does not change with eye length.
evidence: Theoretical model illustrated in Figure 1B

claim: In the equatorial stretching model, angular cone density will increase with eye length.
source: Since the retina is moving further from the secondary nodal point, more cones will fall within a fixed angular area and the angular cone density will increase with eye length.
evidence: Theoretical model illustrated in Figure 1B

claim: In the over-development model, longer eyes will show both increased linear cone density and an even steeper increase in angular cone density.
source: In this scenario, longer eyes will show both increased linear cone density and an even steeper increase in angular cone density.
evidence: Theoretical model illustrated in Figure 1C

claim: Increased linear cone density was observed in the foveas of marmosets that underwent lens-induced eye growth.
source: The model is motivated by observations of increased linear cone density in the foveas of marmosets that underwent lens-induced eye growth (Troilo, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Troilo, 1998

claim: Chui et al. (2008) found a significant decrease (p<0.05) in linear cone density as a function of eye length at 1 mm in all directions except in the nasal retina.
source: Chui et al. (2008) investigated angular and linear cone density at 1 mm and three degrees eccentricity. They found a significant decrease (p<0.05) in linear cone density as a function of eye length at 1 mm (which, by angular distance, is closer to the fovea in a longer eye than in a shorter eye) in all directions except in the nasal retina.
evidence: Supported by citation to Chui et al. (2008)

claim: Chui et al. (2008) found that angular cone density at three degrees increased with eye length, but the trends were not significant.
source: They found that the angular cone density at three degrees (which, by linear distance, is closer to the fovea, in a shorter eye than in a longer eye) increased with eye length, but the trends were not significant.
evidence: Supported by citation to Chui et al. (2008)

claim: Li et al. (2010) found that linear cone density decreased with eye length, but the trends were not significant at the smallest eccentricities (0.1 and 0.2 mm).
source: Li et al. (2010) made similar measures, but closer to the fovea (from 0.10 mm to 0.30 mm eccentricity). They found that linear cone density decreased with eye length, but the trends were not significant at the smallest eccentricities (0.1 and 0.2 mm).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al. (2010)

claim: Li et al. (2010) found that angular cone density trended toward an increase with eye length but none of the trends were significant.
source: When the data were plotted in angular units and angular distance from the fovea, they found that angular cone density trended toward an increase with eye length but none of the trends were significant.
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al. (2010)

claim: Wilk et al. (2017) data showed that linear cone density at the foveal center dropped significantly with increases in axial length.
source: We plotted the data they provided in their paper and found that the linear cone density at the foveal center dropped significantly with increases in axial length, similar to what was found by Li et al. (2010) and Chui et al. (2008)
evidence: Reanalysis of data from Wilk et al. (2017)

claim: Wilk et al. (2017) data showed that angular cone density had no dependency on eye length.
source: but the angular cone density had no dependency on eye length.
evidence: Reanalysis of data from Wilk et al. (2017)

claim: The study included 28 eyes of 16 subjects with a wide range of refractive error and axial length.
source: We report data from 28 eyes of 16 subjects with a wide range of refractive error and axial length.
evidence: Reported in the Results section and detailed in Table 2

claim: The strong correlation between refractive error and eye length (p<0.0001) indicates that the myopia in this cohort was predominantly as a result of axial length.
source: The strong correlation between refractive error and eye length (p<0.0001) indicates that the myopia in this cohort was predominantly as a result of axial length.
evidence: Statistical analysis of biometry data in Table 2

claim: All the cones were resolved with the imaging system.
source: All the cones were resolved with our imaging system.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 3A showing resolved cone mosaic

claim: Subject 10003L has a peak linear density of 204,020 cones/mm².
source: This eye has a peak linear density of 204,020 cones/mm², and a peak angular density of 15,851 cones/deg².
evidence: Measured from AOSLO image shown in Figure 3 and listed in Table 2

claim: Subject 10003L has a peak angular density of 15,851 cones/deg².
source: This eye has a peak linear density of 204,020 cones/mm², and a peak angular density of 15,851 cones/deg².
evidence: Measured from AOSLO image shown in Figure 3 and listed in Table 2

claim: Peak linear density decreases significantly with axial length.
source: Figure 5A reveals that peak linear density decreases significantly with axial length and the trend persists and remains significant from the fovea out to 100 microns eccentricity.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 5A with statistical significance

claim: The trend of decreasing linear density with axial length persists and remains significant from the fovea out to 100 microns eccentricity.
source: Figure 5A reveals that peak linear density decreases significantly with axial length and the trend persists and remains significant from the fovea out to 100 microns eccentricity.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 5A with statistical significance

claim: Axial length accounts for 39% of the variance in the changes in linear cone density.
source: Axial length accounts for 39% of the variance in the changes in linear cone density.
evidence: Statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Peak angular density increases significantly with axial length.
source: Figure 5B shows the opposite trends when plotted in angular units. Peak angular density increases significantly with axial length and the trend persists and remains significant out to 40 arcminutes eccentricity.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 5B with statistical significance

claim: The trend of increasing angular density with axial length persists and remains significant out to 40 arcminutes eccentricity.
source: Peak angular density increases significantly with axial length and the trend persists and remains significant out to 40 arcminutes eccentricity.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 5B with statistical significance

claim: Axial length accounts for 32% of the variance in the changes in angular cone density.
source: Axial length accounts for 32% of the variance in the changes in angular cone density.
evidence: Statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 5B

claim: Although stretching does occur, it is not a simple global expansion and longer eyes have higher sampling density.
source: The plots clearly indicate that although stretching does occur (Figure 5A) it is not a simple global expansion and longer eyes have higher sampling density.
evidence: Inferred from opposite trends in Figure 5A and 5B

claim: The average displacement between PRL and maximum cone density was 6.1 arcminutes and 30.4 microns.
source: We found that the average displacement between PRL and maximum cone density was 6.1 arcminutes and 30.4 microns.
evidence: Calculated from data in Table 2

claim: There was no significant linear relationship found between PRL displacement in either angular or linear units vs. axial length.
source: There was no significant linear relationship found between PRL displacement in either angular or linear units vs. axial length.
evidence: Statistical analysis of PRL displacement data

claim: The PRL was not more displaced in myopes than in emmetropes from the point of peak cone density.
source: Therefore, the PRL was not more displaced in myopes than in emmetropes from the point of peak cone density.
evidence: Inferred from lack of significant relationship between PRL displacement and axial length

claim: Cone density at the PRL shows the same trend with axial length as at the point of maximum cone density.
source: Plots of the cone density at the PRL with axial length show the same trend at the PRL as at the point of maximum cone density (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 6A and B

claim: Fixation stability around the PRL had an average standard deviation of 3.94 arcminutes and 19.84 microns.
source: Fixation stability around the PRL had an average standard deviation of 3.94 arcminutes and 19.84 microns.
evidence: Calculated from fixation data

claim: The average area of the best fitting ellipse containing ~68% of the points in the scatterplot (BCEA) was 50.7 square arcminutes and 1303 square microns.
source: The average area of the best fitting ellipse containing ~68% of the points in the scatterplot (defined as the bivariate contour ellipse area, or BCEA) was 50.7 square arcminutes and 1303 square microns.
evidence: Calculated from fixation data

claim: The plot of BCEA in square microns vs. axial length showed a trend that approached significance (p=0.0596).
source: The plot of BCEA in square microns vs. axial length vs. showed a trend that approached significance (p=0.0596) (Figure 7A)
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 7A

claim: When BCEA was plotted in square arcminutes vs. axial length, the trend was no longer apparent (p=0.364).
source: but when we plotted BCEA in square arcminutes vs. axial length, the trend was no longer apparent (p=0.364) (Figure 7B).
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 7B

claim: If there is any increase in fixational eye movements in microns, it is just a symptom of having a longer eye.
source: In other words, if there is any increase in fixational eye movements in microns, it is just a symptom of having a longer eye.
evidence: Inferred from the difference in significance between linear and angular BCEA measures

claim: This is the first comprehensive study of cones in living eyes at the foveal center.
source: In this paper, we measure the cone density at and near the foveal center and investigate how it changes as a function of axial length. This is the first comprehensive study of cones in living eyes at the foveal center, the area solely responsible for a human's fine spatial vision.
evidence: Stated in Discussion section

claim: The results show that although some expansion does occur (linear cone density decreases with axial length) the angular sampling resolution actually increases, on average, with axial length.
source: Our results show that although some expansion does occur (linear cone density decreases with axial length) the angular sampling resolution actually increases, on average, with axial length.
evidence: Summary of findings from Figure 5

claim: Prior to this study, the relationships between cone density and axial length were only made outside of the fovea, the closest being 0.1 mm, or 0.3 degrees.
source: Prior to this study, the relationships between cone density and axial length were only made outside of the fovea, the closest being 0.1 mm, or 0.3 degrees (Li et al., 2010).
evidence: Comparison with previous literature

claim: The cone density drops precipitously just outside of the location of peak density.
source: Although an eccentricity of 0.3 degrees might seem close, it is noted that the cone density drops precipitously just outside of the location of peak density (Curcio et al., 1990)
evidence: Supported by citation to Curcio et al., 1990

claim: Human vision drops precipitously just outside of the location of peak cone density.
source: Although an eccentricity of 0.3 degrees might seem close, it is noted that the cone density drops precipitously just outside of the location of peak density (Curcio et al., 1990) as does human vision (Poletti et al., 2013) (Rossi and Roorda, 2010b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Poletti et al., 2013 and Rossi and Roorda, 2010b

claim: Eye length accounts for anywhere between 31% and 39% of the variance in cone density at the foveal center.
source: There are other factors that govern peak cone density, however; eye length accounts for anywhere between 31% and 39% of the variance in cone density at the foveal center.
evidence: Statistical analysis of variance in cone density data

claim: The finding that the slopes of cone density vs. axial length are in opposite directions when plotted in linear (negative slope) and angular (positive slope) units supports an eye growth model that lies between the global expansion model and an equatorial stretching model.
source: Our finding that the slopes of cone density vs. axial length are in opposite directions when plotted in linear (negative slope) and angular (positive slope) units, supports an eye growth model that lies between the global expansion model and an equatorial stretching model.
evidence: Inference from data in Figure 5 compared to theoretical models in Figure 1

claim: Previous studies from Li et al. (2010) and Chui et al. (2008) leaned in the same direction as the current study's findings.
source: Previous studies from our lab (Li et al., 2010) and also from Chui et al. (2008) leaned in the same direction.
evidence: Comparison with previous literature

claim: Atchison et al. (2004) used magnetic resonance imaging and found that eyeball dimensions in axial myopes are variable but are generally larger in all directions with a weak tendency to be preferentially greater in the axial direction.
source: Specifically, Atchison et al. (2004) used magnetic resonance imaging and found that eyeball dimensions in axial myopes are variable but are generally larger in all directions with a weak tendency to be preferentially greater in the axial direction.
evidence: Supported by citation to Atchison et al. (2004)

claim: Atchison et al. (2004)'s reported eye growth patterns lie between that illustrated for the global expansion and equatorial stretching models.
source: Their reported eye growth patterns lie between that illustrated for the global expansion and equatorial stretching models in Figure 1.
evidence: Inference comparing Atchison et al. (2004) findings to theoretical models

claim: The current study's results differ from Wilk et al. (2017) whose data support a global expansion model.
source: Our results differ from Wilk et al. (2017) whose data support a global expansion model (i.e. there is no detectable change in angular cone density with axial length; Figure 2B).
evidence: Comparison with Wilk et al. (2017) data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Wilk et al. (2017) study did not set out to address the same question and the number of subjects with long axial lengths was disproportionately low.
source: But it is important to point out that their study did not set out to address the same question and the number of subjects with long axial lengths was disproportionately low.
evidence: Critical evaluation of Wilk et al. (2017) study design

claim: Troilo (1998) observed higher cone packing densities in experimentally enlarged marmoset eyes compared to normal eyes in the fovea.
source: Our results also differ from Troilo (1998) who studied retinal cell topography in a marmoset animal myopia model. Higher cone packing densities were observed in the experimentally enlarged eyes compared to normal eyes in the fovea.
evidence: Supported by citation to Troilo (1998)

claim: Troilo (1998)'s result followed the overdevelopment model.
source: Their result followed the overdevelopment model, which is the reason why we included it as one of the possible outcomes of our study.
evidence: Inference from Troilo (1998) findings

claim: The overdevelopment model is an extension of Springer's model of development.
source: In fact, the overdevelopment model is an extension of Springer's model of development (Springer and Hendrickson, 2004), which offers a biomechanical explanation for how cone packing increases at the foveal center in a developing eye.
evidence: Supported by citation to Springer and Hendrickson, 2004

claim: The current study's data do not support the overdevelopment model.
source: While our data do not support the overdevelopment model, it does not preclude the existence of biomechanical factors working in opposition to simple global expansion.
evidence: Inference from data in Figure 5 compared to theoretical models

claim: The current study's data do not preclude the existence of biomechanical factors working in opposition to simple global expansion.
source: While our data do not support the overdevelopment model, it does not preclude the existence of biomechanical factors working in opposition to simple global expansion.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of findings

claim: Poorer performance by myopes on resolution tasks cannot be explained by a decrease in photoreceptor sampling.
source: The fact that angular cone density (visual sampling resolution) increases with eye length (myopia), at the peak density and at the PRL, means that poorer performance by myopes on resolution tasks cannot be explained by a decrease in photoreceptor sampling.
evidence: Inference from findings that angular density increases with axial length

claim: The deficit in myopic visual performance must arise at a post-receptoral level.
source: The deficit must arise at a post-receptoral level.
evidence: Inference from ruling out photoreceptor sampling as cause

claim: Atchison et al. (2006) suggested that abnormal eye growth may be associated with a loss of ganglion cells.
source: Atchison et al. (2006) suggested that abnormal eye growth may be associated with a loss of ganglion cells.
evidence: Supported by citation to Atchison et al. (2006)

claim: If ganglion cells pool signals from multiple cones, then they will impose the retinal sampling limit and reduce certain aspects of visual performance.
source: Alternately, if ganglion cells pool signals from multiple cones, then they will impose the retinal sampling limit and reduce certain aspects of visual performance (acuity, for example).
evidence: Theoretical reasoning about neural connectivity

claim: Recent electron microscopy studies of a human fovea have revealed extensive convergence and divergence connections between photoreceptors and ganglion cells.
source: Recent electron microscopy studies of a human fovea have revealed extensive convergence and divergence connections between photoreceptors and ganglion cells, albeit in an eye from an individual who was born prematurely (Dacey, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dacey, 2018

claim: Rossi et al. (2007) and Coletta and Watson (2006) raised the possibility that myopes might have become desensitized to high frequency information as a result of having less exposure to a high contrast visual environment.
source: To explain why low myopes did not perform as well on an acuity task as emmetropes, even after correction or bypassing of high order aberrations, Rossi et al. (2007) and Coletta and Watson (2006) both raised the possibility that myopes might have become desensitized to high frequency information (low level myopic amblyopia) as a result of having less exposure to a high contrast visual environment.
evidence: Supported by citations to Rossi et al. (2007) and Coletta and Watson (2006)

claim: One myope in a follow up study by Rossi and Roorda (2010a) never reached the acuity levels of emmetropes in the same study.
source: In this case, it might be possible to train myopes to take advantage of their higher sampling resolution, but one myope in a follow up study by Rossi and Roorda (2010a) never reached the acuity levels of emmetropes in the same study.
evidence: Supported by citation to Rossi and Roorda (2010a)

claim: Curcio et al. (1990) found a large range of peak foveal cone densities with an average of 199,000 cones/mm2.
source: Curcio et al. (1990) measured spatial density of cones and rods in eight explanted whole-mounted human retinas. They found a large range of peak foveal cone densities with an average of 199,000 cones/mm2.
evidence: Supported by citation to Curcio et al. (1990)

claim: The current study's range of peak cone densities measured over a 10 arcmin (~50 micron) sampling window was 118,491 to 204,020 with an average of 163,242 cones/mm2.
source: Our range of peak cone densities measured over a 10 arcmin (~50 micron) sampling window was 118,491 to 204,020 with an average of 163,242 cones/mm2.
evidence: Calculated from data in Table 2

claim: When peak cone density was averaged over a circular aperture of 7.5 arcminutes, the study measured peak linear cone densities ranging from 123,611 to 208,606 with an average of 166,854 cones/mm2.
source: When we averaged the peak cone density over a circular aperture of 7.5 arcminutes which was more similar to the sampling window that Curcio et al. (1990) used to compute density, we measured peak linear cone densities ranging from 123,611 to 208,606 with an average of 166,854 cones/mm2.
evidence: Reanalysis of data with different sampling window

claim: Zhang et al. (2015) reported an average peak density of 168,162 cones/mm2 in 40 eyes.
source: Zhang et al. (2015) reported an average peak density of 168,162 cones/mm2 in 40 eyes although they used a much smaller 5 × 5 micron sampling window to measure the peak.
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al. (2015)

claim: Wilk et al. (2017) reported an average peak density of 145,900 cones/mm2 in 22 eyes using a 37 × 37 micron sampling window.
source: Wilk et al. (2017) reported an average peak density of 145,900 cones/mm2 in 22 eyes using a 37 × 37 micron sampling window
evidence: Supported by citation to Wilk et al. (2017)

claim: Li et al. (2010) reported an average peak density of 150,412 cones/mm2 in four eyes over a sampling window encompassing 150 cones.
source: Li et al. (2010) reported an average peak density of 150,412 cones/mm2 in four eyes over a sampling window encompassing 150 cones (approximately 37 micron diameter at the foveal center).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al. (2010)

claim: All reports of cone densities from adaptive optics studies in living eyes are lower than reports from histology.
source: All reports of cone densities from adaptive optics studies in living eyes are lower than reports from histology.
evidence: Comparison of current and previous AO studies with Curcio et al. (1990) histology

claim: The excised tissue in Curcio et al. (1990) may have undergone more shrinkage than estimated.
source: Two possible reasons for this are (i) the excised tissue in Curcio et al. (1990) underwent more shrinkage than estimated
evidence: Speculation about methodological differences

claim: The adaptive optics reports may be subject to selection bias, where individuals with the highest angular cone densities might have been excluded because the images were less well resolved.
source: or (ii) the adaptive optics reports are subject to selection bias, where individuals with the highest angular cone densities might have been excluded because the image were less well resolved rendering the cones images too difficult to label with confidence.
evidence: Speculation about potential selection bias

claim: The study attempted to image 73 eyes from 46 subjects and only succeeded in resolving cones across a sufficiently large region at and around the fovea in 28 of them.
source: In our study, we attempted to image 73 eyes from 46 subjects and only succeeded in resolving cones across a sufficiently large region at and around the fovea in 28 of them.
evidence: Description of study methodology and success rate

claim: Images from four eyes (three subjects) were not analyzed because their refractive errors were too high (all above –8D).
source: Images from four eyes (three subjects) were not analyzed because their refractive errors were too high (all above –8D) and we ran into the limits of the deformable mirror's dynamic range.
evidence: Description of exclusion criteria

claim: Like Curcio et al. (1990) and Zhang et al. (2015), the current study found steeper drops in cone density in the superior and inferior directions compared to the nasal and temporal directions.
source: Like Curcio et al. (1990) and Zhang et al. (2015) we found steeper drops in cone density in the superior and inferior directions compared to the nasal and temporal directions.
evidence: Comparison with previous studies, shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 2

claim: The distance of the PRL from the foveal center for the current study (mean 30.4 microns; range 5.7–83.7; n = 28) roughly agrees with those of Wilk et al. (2017) (mean 63 microns; range 20–263; n = 22).
source: The distance of the PRL from the foveal center for our study (mean 30.4 microns; range 5.7–83.7; n = 28) roughly agrees with those of Wilk et al. (2017) (mean 63 microns; range 20–263; n = 22)
evidence: Comparison with Wilk et al. (2017)

claim: The distance of the PRL from the foveal center for the current study roughly agrees with Li et al. (2010) (mean 34 microns; range 3–92; n = 18).
source: The distance of the PRL from the foveal center for our study (mean 30.4 microns; range 5.7–83.7; n = 28) roughly agrees with those of Wilk et al. (2017) (mean 63 microns; range 20–263; n = 22), Li et al. (2010) (mean 34 microns; range 3–92; n = 18)
evidence: Comparison with Li et al. (2010)

claim: The distance of the PRL from the foveal center for the current study roughly agrees with Putnam et al. (2005) (mean 17; range 11–23; n = 5).
source: The distance of the PRL from the foveal center for our study (mean 30.4 microns; range 5.7–83.7; n = 28) roughly agrees with those of Wilk et al. (2017) (mean 63 microns; range 20–263; n = 22), Li et al. (2010) (mean 34 microns; range 3–92; n = 18) and Putnam et al. (2005) (mean 17; range 11–23; n = 5).
evidence: Comparison with Putnam et al. (2005)

claim: The cone array imposes the first retinal sampling limit to human spatial vision.
source: The cone array imposes the first retinal sampling limit to human spatial vision (MacLeod et al., 1992; Williams, 1985)
evidence: Supported by citations to MacLeod et al., 1992; Williams, 1985

claim: For the densities reported in the current study, the potential spatial frequency resolution limits range from 59.1 to 74.01 cyc/deg (average: 64.9 cyc/deg) at the peak density.
source: For the densities reported here, the potential spatial frequency resolution limits range from 59.1 to 74.01 cyc/deg (average: 64.9 cyc/deg) at the peak density
evidence: Calculated from cone density data

claim: For the densities reported in the current study, the potential spatial frequency resolution limits range from 50.4 to 71.9 cyc/deg (average: 62.5 cyc/deg) at the PRL.
source: and 50.4 to 71.9 cyc/deg (average: 62.5 cyc/deg) at the PRL.
evidence: Calculated from cone density data

claim: The potential acuities based on cone density range from 20/11.9 to 20/8.1.
source: These correspond to potential acuities ranging from 20/11.9 to 20/8.1 (based on the primary spatial frequency of the three bars of a Snellen E).
evidence: Calculated from spatial frequency resolution limits

claim: The cone frequency cut-offs are higher than almost all the interferometric acuity limits reported by Coletta and Watson (2006), even for the emmetropic subjects.
source: The cone frequency cut-offs are higher than almost all the interferometric acuity limits reported by Coletta and Watson (2006), even for the emmetropic subjects.
evidence: Comparison with Coletta and Watson (2006) findings

claim: The acuities calculated from cone density are in the range of those measured from emmetropic subjects after adaptive optics correction by Rossi et al. (2007).
source: The acuities are, however, in the range of those measured from emmetropic subjects after adaptive optics correction by Rossi et al. (2007).
evidence: Comparison with Rossi et al. (2007) findings

claim: The cone center-to-center spacing ranges from 0.59 to 0.47 arcminutes at the peak density.
source: The cone center-to-center spacing ranges from 0.59 to 0.47 arcminutes at the peak density
evidence: Calculated from cone density data

claim: The cone center-to-center spacing ranges from 0.69 to 0.48 arcminutes at the PRL.
source: and from 0.69 to 0.48 arcminutes at the PRL.
evidence: Calculated from cone density data

claim: The latest generation of adaptive optics ophthalmoscopes are making it easier to measure structure and function of cone photoreceptors at the foveal center.
source: Measuring structure and function of cone photoreceptors at the foveal center – the most important region of the human retina – has been one of the more challenging endeavors in vision science. Fortunately, the latest generation of adaptive optics ophthalmoscopes are making it easier and are facilitating new discoveries within this retinal region.
evidence: General statement about technological advances

claim: The pattern of how cone density changes with eye growth lands somewhere between the global expansion and equatorial stretching models.
source: The pattern of how cone density changes with eye growth lands somewhere between the global expansion and equatorial stretching models.
